extracted.intended_audience: sanitary engineers, public-health officers, municipal engineers, and homeowners planning or constructing domestic water supplies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, protecting, testing, and constructing water-collection points and small-scale water-works for houses and villages (wells, springs, brooks, reservoirs), with sanitary inspection and quality criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineral content / hardness (good water)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good waters contain from twenty to one hundred grains per gallon of mineral salts; if the amount is much in excess of one hundred parts, the water is noticeably 'hard,' and this may increase to a point where the water cannot be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mineral waters (e.g., containing more than 100 grains per gallon of salts such as magnesium sulphate or sodium phosphate) are not fit for constant drinking though an occasional glass may be medicinal. Use the 20–100 grains/gallon band as a guideline for 'good' drinking water; above ~100 consider hardness treatment or alternate sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health effects of hard vs soft water
rubrics_metrics.description: Within reasonable limits there is little to choose between a hard and soft water for drinking purposes, although a change from a soft water to a hard, or vice versa, usually produces temporary derangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes conflicting reports (French and Vienna commissioners favor moderate hardness; English commissioner found mortality practically uninfluenced). There is no satisfactory proof linking hard water to diseases like calculus, cancer, goiter, or cretinism; evaluate claims cautiously and not as absolute disqualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soap loss / economic cost of hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a hard water is used, a certain amount of soap is required to neutralize the hardness before the soap is effective, at the rate of about 2 ounces of soap to 100 gallons of water for each part of calcium carbonate per gallon (or about 3 ounces per 10,000 gallons per part per million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Whipple's cost expression H/100 = D (H = hardness in parts per million; D = cost in cents per 1000 gallons). Example calculations (Canisteo 162.8 ppm → 1.6 cents/1000 gal; Catskill 22.1 ppm → 0.2 cent/1000 gal) illustrate economic impact; account for actual fraction of water neutralized when estimating real costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetable pollution: aesthetic vs sanitary significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetable pollution (decayed leaves, roots, bark) yields brownish discoloration and a slight sweetish taste and appears soft (low mineral solids); such water usually can be used for drinking without serious health consequences, though it is aesthetically objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical analyses show large amounts of nitrogenous matter which may suggest pollution, but if source is swamp vegetation, danger to health is not necessarily present. Consider aesthetic treatment (e.g., watershed drainage) separately from sanitary condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal pollution: presence of domestic animals and manure
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal pollution results from domestic animals, manure spread on fields draining into brooks, or barns and barnyards close to the water; this organic matter is vastly more objectionable than vegetable-origin matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and evaluate by personal inspection of the watershed: note pasture, manured slopes, proximity of barns and outbuildings. If a brook flows through pasture or manured gullies, the water is probably unfit for drinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sewage/privy contamination as highest sanitary risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Leachings and washings from privies and cesspools, carrying germs of contagious diseases, are most to be dreaded; a privy built so that drainage runs into a stream risks deadly pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inspection shows sewage entering the stream, the sewage should be diverted, spread over ground away from the stream, or purified before discharge; otherwise the creek cannot be used. Presence of privies above intake is sufficient cause to rule out a surface supply for domestic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watershed inspection practices
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate a stream for drinking-water use, the first step is to examine carefully the area draining into the stream to detect all opportunities for animal wastes or sewage to enter the stream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection must be personal and thorough—check points of discharge of every house sewer on the watershed without relying on occupants' statements; locate barns, pig-pens, privies, cesspools, manure fields, slaughter-houses, and drainage patterns to determine suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privy and cesspool siting and construction standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Privies should be as far back from the banks as possible; water-tight boxes can prevent surface wash-in if periodically emptied. Cesspools are generally not dangerous if located fifty feet or more from the stream and if no overflow occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where necessary, provide water-tight vaults (e.g., brick eight inches thick with eight-inch brick floors laid with cement and inside surfaces lined with at least one inch of cement) to prevent seepage. The Syracuse collection system is cited as an example of effective watershed protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well protection: masonry, depth, and cover
rubrics_metrics.description: To protect a well from gross pollution: build the well wall of water-tight masonry so surface wash cannot enter except at a depth of at least six feet; carry this masonry above the surface at least six inches and cover the well with a water-tight floor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precautions will stop about nine tenths of pollution in isolated wells. Ensure pump waste cannot wash into the well and that openings through the cover are secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of underground water flow and cesspool proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Underground water flow may carry contaminating matter from cesspools into wells; cesspools that extend to the same water level as a well can contaminate it, whereas shallow cesspools are less objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect groundwater flow direction by simple tests (e.g., throw a gallon of kerosene into a test hole at suspected point and check for kerosene in the well). Do not site cesspools at same level and up-gradient of wells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory testing thresholds and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Have water examined by a chemist for ammonia and other indicators of organic pollution; test for number of bacteria—'a well of spring water which contains more than about fifty in a cubic centimeter is a suspicious water.' Presence of the colon bacillus, even in very small quantities, strongly presumes human/animal fecal pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprete counts in context: surface waters may show higher total bacteria (two or three hundred per cc) yet be harmless depending on types. Treat any detection of colon bacillus as serious and as evidence the source is not fit for drinking without treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rule for surface supplies: filtration or protected ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: It is out of the question for any surface water-supply to be pure; no surface supply will be considered satisfactory unless the water is filtered, or the watershed is owned and access restricted so dwellings and cultivation are prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer secured, privately owned watershed with restored primeval forest where feasible; otherwise plan for filtration or discard the supply if all known organic pollutions cannot be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection-method selection based on frost risk and supply variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple methods (galvanized iron pipe laid to spring with strainer, pipe on lake bottom with strainer, projecting pipe into stream) are acceptable provided supply need is not in winter and flow is adequate; where frost occurs or supply is inadequate, more elaborate construction (pipe below frost line, spring inclosure, storage) is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pipe is buried below frost line throughout its length; roof and protect springs to prevent surface wash-in; avoid encasing pipe in structures that lead to freezing (example of stone wall built around pipe causing freeze). Provide storage if stream flow is periodic or insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring reservoir construction standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Spring reservoirs should be built of concrete (or heavy barrel/sewer pipe in a pinch), usually digging 4–5 feet deep; leave holes on the side from which the spring enters; connect with agricultural tile drains to both drain ground and add volume; size reservoir for required storage (a family of ten ≈ 500 gallons → one day's supply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spring always overflows, a small sewer pipe may suffice; if storage is needed size for number of days' storage. Wall thickness: ~9 inches for 6–8 ft depth, 12 inches for greater depths. Roof: concrete flat slab 6 inches thick with embedded iron rods—½-inch rods spaced ~1 ft for small spans, ¾-inch up to 9 ft, 1-inch up to 12 ft; include manhole opening protected with iron cover; place outlet pipe about halfway between top and bottom; provide drainpipe with valve box. Concrete mix suggested: 1 part cement to 5 parts gravel, or 1:4 stone and 2 sand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting springs from surface drainage and runoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Where springs lie in depressions or at low points that catch surface drainage, protect them by banking earth around the spring and providing alternative drainage (e.g., a pipe) so surface water passes above it; roof springs when possible to prevent surface contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spring is in a ravine that is subject to torrent flows carrying road pollution, either divert the gulley water or dig and roof the spring so it cannot be washed through. Use drainage tiles and banks to keep surface runoff away from the spring.
